description:
Bare whole-axis references (`=A:A`, `=A:C`, `=1:2`) used as the whole formula, i.e. as a spilling expression rather than as a function argument. Every case declares its own `formula_cell`, because the observable result depends on where the formula sits.
Excel 365 treats a bare whole-axis reference like any other bare range: the value is the array of the *declared* rectangle — rows 1..1048576 for a column span, columns A..XFD for a row span — and it spills from the formula cell. Nothing is trimmed to the populated extent, and cells with no content spill as 0. Three consequences are directly observable and are what this suite pins:

  * the rectangle must fit inside the grid measured from the formula
    cell, so a whole-column reference only spills from row 1 and a
    whole-row reference only from column A; anywhere else is `#SPILL!`;
  * any occupied cell anywhere in that rectangle blocks the spill, even
    one far below or far to the right of the populated data, which is
    what shows the footprint is the full declared rectangle;
  * a formula that sits inside the axis it references is a circular
    reference, so it never spills at all.

The four full-rectangle spills use `capture: shape`: their results are far larger than the cell-by-cell capture ceiling (the smallest is 16,384 cells against a 4,096 ceiling), so the golden records the dynamic-array shape plus the listed sample cells instead of every cell. Excel answers them normally; only the recording differs.
The remaining seven are recorded cell by cell and are currently registered in tests/divergence.yaml. Each `expect` block below is Excel's observed answer; deleting an entry and regenerating this suite turns the corresponding case back into a verified golden.

cases.skipped: =A:A at A1 with column A otherwise empty: the rectangle fits and the runway is clear, so only the cycle stops the spill. Nothing else in column A holds a formula, so the formula cell is the sole member of the cycle and Excel seeds it with 0. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy.

=5:5 at A5 with row 5 otherwise empty: same isolation on the row axis. Nothing else in row 5 holds a formula, so the formula cell is the sole member of the cycle and Excel seeds it with 0. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy.

=A:A+0 at A1 with column A otherwise empty: the formula cell is the sole member of the cycle and Excel seeds it with 0, as for the bare =A:A. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy (circular_reference_iterative_off_returns_ref).

=SUM(C:C*1) at C1 with column C otherwise empty: the formula cell is the sole member of the cycle and Excel seeds it with 0. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy (circular_reference_iterative_off_returns_ref).

=ROWS(G:G+0) at G1: G:G+0 reads the formula cell, so the cell is in a cycle; Excel seeds it and ROWS reports the declared 1048576 rows. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy (circular_reference_iterative_off_returns_ref).

=A:A at A1 with A2/A3 occupied: circular and blocked at once, and Excel answers 0 -- it decides the cycle before the blocking check. A2 and A3 hold literal data, not formulas, so the formula cell is the only member of this cycle and its 0 is a single readable value rather than one term of a cascade. Formulon returns #REF! per its cycle policy. The control case with the formula cell outside the referenced column is a live golden and reports #SPILL!, so the pair pins the ordering rather than the blocking.

SUM(Sheet2!A:A+Sheet2!1:1): a whole column plus a whole row broadcasts to the full 1,048,576 x 16,384 grid. Excel answers 0 for it (measured; the rule behind the 0 is not identified). Formulon has no single repeated tail for a two-axis result, so it would have to expand ~1.7e10 cells and refuses with #NUM! at the derived-array ceiling, as for any other oversized array.
